Among the proteins listed, CSF1R stands out as the most biologically relevant to depression because its functions intersect directly with neuroimmune and inflammatory mechanisms that are increasingly recognized as central components of depressive pathophysiology. CSF1R signaling regulates monocyte/macrophage biology and promotes the release of pro-inflammatory chemokines, which is notable because chronic low-grade inflammation and altered innate immune activation have been repeatedly associated with major depressive disorder. Of particular importance, the annotation indicates that CSF1R may contribute to the development of microglia in the central nervous system. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain and are strongly implicated in stress responses, synaptic remodeling, neuroinflammation, and altered neuroplasticity, all of which are mechanistically linked to depression. In addition, CSF1R activates extracellular signal regulated kinase 1 and 2, c Jun N terminal kinase, phosphoinositide 3 kinase and protein kinase B, SRC family kinases, and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, pathways that are relevant to cellular survival, inflammatory transcriptional programs, and neuroplastic processes that are often dysregulated in depressive illness. The receptor’s ability to promote cell migration, cytoskeletal reorganization, and inflammatory signaling further supports its potential role in shaping brain-immune communication. Therefore, CSF1R is especially important in the present list because it plausibly connects peripheral immune activation with central microglial function, providing a mechanistic bridge between inflammation and depression-related neural dysfunction.

In comparison with CSF1R, CD4 appears to have a less direct connection to depression, but it may still be relevant through its role in adaptive immunity and infection-associated inflammatory states. CD4 is less directly connected to depression than CSF1R, but it remains potentially relevant because it is central to host-pathogen interactions and adaptive immune function. Its principal annotated role here concerns viral entry, particularly as the primary receptor for HIV-1 and as a receptor for HHV-7. This is important in the context of depression because chronic viral infection, immune dysregulation, and sustained inflammatory activation can contribute to depressive symptoms, especially in medically ill populations. HIV infection, for example, is associated with neuroinflammation, immune activation, and neuropsychiatric complications, including depression. Thus, while CD4 itself is not described here as a canonical depression-related signaling molecule, its involvement in infections that can alter immune homeostasis and central nervous system function gives it an indirect but meaningful connection to depression biology. Relative to CSF1R, however, the evidence from the provided annotation supports CD4 primarily as a context-dependent contributor through infection-associated inflammatory and neuroimmune mechanisms rather than as a direct regulator of depression-relevant pathways.[PubMed:12089508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089508) [PubMed:16331979](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16331979) [PubMed:2214026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2214026) [PubMed:9641677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9641677) [PubMed:17346169](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17346169) [PubMed:7909607](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7909607)

### regulation of lipid metabolic process (GO:0019216) 

Regulation of lipid metabolic process comprises all mechanisms that increase, decrease, or otherwise shape the synthesis, modification, transport, storage, and degradation of lipids. Lipids include fatty acids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, sterols, glycerolipids, and their bioactive derivatives. Because lipids are fundamental structural components of cellular membranes, major substrates for energy storage, and precursors of signaling molecules, their metabolism is tightly controlled across multiple organs, including the brain, liver, adipose tissue, immune system, and endocrine tissues. In the nervous system, regulation of lipid metabolic process is essential for membrane fluidity, synaptic vesicle formation, myelination, mitochondrial function, receptor localization, and intracellular signaling. This pathway also intersects with inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis activity, insulin sensitivity, and neurotransmitter systems such as serotonin, dopamine, glutamate, and gamma aminobutyric acid. Disturbance of lipid metabolic regulation can therefore alter neuronal resilience, neuroinflammation, energy homeostasis, and synaptic plasticity, all of which are biologically relevant to depression.

Against this biological background, the currently supplied evidence should be interpreted with caution. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a literature-supported pathway to depression cannot be attributed to the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, from a biological perspective, regulation of lipid metabolic process is plausibly related to depression because altered lipid homeostasis can influence several mechanisms repeatedly implicated in depressive illness. Abnormal handling of fatty acids and membrane phospholipids may change membrane composition and receptor function, thereby affecting neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity. Dysregulated sphingolipid and sterol metabolism may promote neuroinflammatory signaling, oxidative injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired cellular stress responses, each of which can contribute to reduced neuronal adaptability and mood disturbance. In addition, systemic alterations in lipid metabolism are closely linked to obesity, insulin resistance, and chronic low-grade inflammation, conditions that frequently co-occur with depression and may exacerbate depressive symptoms through immune, endocrine, and metabolic communication between the periphery and the brain. However, because no specific publications were supplied, these statements should be interpreted as a general mechanistic synthesis rather than a conclusion directly supported by the provided reference list.

Building on this general mechanistic context, the enrichment result provides a more focused view of how this pathway may intersect with the depression-associated protein set. There were 9 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway regulation of lipid metabolic process, a biological process that governs the synthesis, modification, transport, storage, and degradation of multiple lipid classes, including fatty acids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, sterols, glycerolipids, and bioactive lipid derivatives. In the context of depression, this enrichment is biologically notable because lipid regulation influences several central systems that are quantitatively relevant to neuronal and systemic homeostasis, including membrane composition, synaptic vesicle dynamics, myelination, mitochondrial energy handling, receptor localization, inflammatory signaling, oxidative balance, hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis activity, insulin sensitivity, and neurotransmitter pathways involving serotonin, dopamine, glutamate, and gamma aminobutyric acid. The identification of 9 proteins within this pathway indicates that a measurable subset of the depression-associated protein set converges on lipid regulatory biology, supporting the interpretation that altered control of lipid metabolism may contribute to depression through effects on neuronal resilience, neuroinflammation, energy homeostasis, and synaptic plasticity.

RARRES2 stands out as one of the most relevant proteins for depression because it directly links adipose biology, immune signaling, metabolic dysfunction, and vascular regulation, all of which are increasingly implicated in depressive disorders. Its role as an adipokine that modulates lipid and glucose metabolism is notable because depression frequently co-occurs with obesity, insulin resistance, and other metabolic abnormalities. Equally important, RARRES2 has pronounced immunomodulatory activity: it recruits plasmacytoid dendritic cells, macrophages, and natural killer cells via CMKLR1, and can promote secretion of pro-inflammatory adipokines that impair systemic metabolic function and insulin sensitivity. Chronic low-grade inflammation is a well-established mechanistic contributor to depression, particularly in patients with metabolic syndrome or atypical depression. At the same time, the protein also has context-dependent anti-inflammatory vascular effects through inhibition of nuclear factor kappa B and CRK and p38 signaling and activation of AKT1 and NOS3, suggesting that dysregulation of RARRES2 signaling could influence endothelial dysfunction and neurovascular health, both of which have been associated with depressive symptomatology. Thus, RARRES2 is especially important because it integrates immune-metabolic and vascular pathways that may shape vulnerability to depression and its systemic comorbidities.

In parallel with this immune-metabolic interface, the next protein points more directly toward central neuroimmune regulation. TREM2-related signaling is highly relevant to depression because it maps directly onto neuroimmune and microglial mechanisms that are now central to contemporary models of depressive pathophysiology. The most compelling aspect is its role in microglia, where it is required for phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons and for regulation of superoxide production during brain development, and where it can promote pro-inflammatory responses following nerve injury. Microglial activation, excessive synaptic and cellular pruning, oxidative stress, and persistent neuroinflammation have all been implicated in depression, particularly in stress-related, neurodegenerative, and inflammation-associated forms of the disorder. In addition, TREM2-associated signaling affects dendritic cell maturation, cytokine regulation, and interleukin 10 production, indicating broader control of innate immune tone. These functions suggest that altered TREM2 pathway activity could influence depressive phenotypes through maladaptive neuroimmune activation, impaired clearance of cellular debris, and altered inflammatory resolution. This protein therefore stands out as a plausible bridge between peripheral immune dysregulation and central nervous system inflammatory processes relevant to depression.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

Extending this immunological perspective, the following protein may contribute more broadly to inflammatory cell recruitment and immune communication. TNF is potentially relevant to depression primarily because of its chemotactic immune function through CCR6, which implicates it in leukocyte trafficking and inflammatory cell recruitment. Although the provided annotation emphasizes antimicrobial activity, the more depression-relevant feature is its ability to attract immature dendritic cells and memory T cells, cell populations that participate in adaptive and innate immune crosstalk. Depression has been strongly associated with immune activation, altered T-cell phenotypes, and elevated inflammatory mediators, and proteins that regulate immune-cell migration may contribute to the maintenance of chronic inflammatory states. The antimicrobial activity is also of interest because host-defense peptides and inflammatory mediators can shape mucosal and systemic immune homeostasis, potentially affecting the gut-brain and skin-brain axes, both of which have emerging links to mood disorders. Overall, TNF is not as directly compelling as RARRES2 or TREM2 in the present list, but its role in immune-cell chemotaxis makes it a plausible contributor to inflammatory mechanisms relevant to depression.[PubMed:10837369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10837369) [PubMed:9202117](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9202117) [PubMed:30050988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30050988) [PubMed:10521347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10521347) [PubMed:20068036](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20068036) 

Shifting from immune trafficking to vascular and neuroendocrine regulation, ADM may add another layer to the pathway interpretation. ADM is of interest in depression because adrenomedullin signaling is broadly involved in vascular tone, stress biology, and neuroendocrine regulation, even though the provided annotation is limited to receptor usage. Its preferential signaling through CALCRL and RAMP2 may be particularly relevant because vascular dysfunction, endothelial stress, and altered neurovascular coupling have been implicated in subsets of depression, especially late-life and inflammation-associated depression. In addition, peptide systems that regulate vascular homeostasis often intersect with stress-response pathways and blood-brain barrier function, both of which may influence mood regulation. While the present functional description does not provide disease-specific mechanistic detail, ADM still stands out as a potentially relevant upstream signaling molecule in depression because neurovascular and peripheral cardiovascular abnormalities are common in depressive illness and may contribute to symptom persistence or treatment resistance.

A related but distinct aspect of lipid regulation involves intracellular cholesterol handling and lysosomal biology, which brings attention to NPC2. NPC2 is relevant to depression because cholesterol trafficking and lysosomal function are increasingly recognized as important for neuronal membrane biology, synaptic function, and neuroinflammatory regulation. The protein’s core role in transferring cholesterol to NPC1 for lysosomal export suggests that disruption of NPC2 could alter membrane composition, receptor organization, and intracellular signaling in neurons and glia. Such disturbances may affect synaptic plasticity, which is a central biological substrate of depression. Moreover, lysosomal dysfunction and defective lipid handling can amplify cellular stress responses and inflammatory signaling, thereby intersecting with pathways implicated in mood disorders. The secreted form’s influence on systemic cholesterol transport also suggests a possible connection to metabolic states that are epidemiologically associated with depression. Although NPC2 is not a canonical depression gene, its function places it within the broader lipid-metabolic and lysosomal framework that may modulate risk for neuropsychiatric disease.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

In addition to lipid handling and lysosomal trafficking, antigen presentation may represent another route through which this enriched set could connect to depression-related biology. CD74 is potentially relevant to depression because it is a key regulator of major histocompatibility complex class two antigen presentation, placing it at the center of adaptive immune activation. Immune dysregulation, including altered antigen presentation and sustained inflammatory signaling, has been repeatedly linked to depression, particularly in patients with autoimmune disease, chronic infection, or elevated peripheral inflammatory markers. By controlling peptide loading onto major histocompatibility complex class two complexes, CD74 influences how antigens are presented to CD4-positive T cells, thereby shaping downstream cytokine responses and immune-cell activation states. These processes can affect systemic inflammation and, indirectly, neuroimmune communication. Although the annotation does not describe direct neurobiological roles, CD74 remains noteworthy because antigen-presentation pathways are increasingly considered part of the immunological architecture that may predispose to or sustain depressive symptoms.

Finally, beyond immune and metabolic signaling, the enriched protein set also includes a factor with possible relevance to transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation. PSAP is noteworthy in depression primarily because of its functions in ribonucleic acid processing, epigenetic repression, and apoptosis-related splicing. The ability of PSAP-containing complexes to regulate messenger ribonucleic acid splicing, including the balance of BCL2L1 and Bcl-X isoforms, is potentially important because stress-related disorders are associated with altered neuronal survival, synaptic remodeling, and transcriptomic dysregulation. Its participation in SIN3 and histone deacetylase 1-mediated transcriptional repression also makes it relevant to epigenetic models of depression, in which chromatin remodeling and transcriptional silencing contribute to persistent changes in neural function after chronic stress. Although the evidence provided here is mechanistic rather than disease-specific, PSAP stands out as a plausible regulator of molecular programs that influence cellular resilience, apoptosis, and long-term transcriptional adaptation, all of which are biologically relevant to depression.

### virus receptor activity (GO:0001618) 

Virus receptor activity refers to the molecular function by which a host cell surface molecule binds a structural component of a virus and enables viral attachment, membrane fusion, endocytosis, or other entry processes that permit infection of the cell. This functional category is fundamentally centered on host factors that act as portals for viral invasion, including proteins, glycoproteins, and, in some contexts, other membrane-associated molecules that determine viral tropism, tissue specificity, and the efficiency of infection. From a biological perspective, virus receptor activity is not a signaling pathway in the classical sense, but rather a host cell entry function that may initiate downstream consequences such as innate immune activation, inflammatory signaling, cellular stress responses, and tissue injury once infection is established. In the nervous system and in peripheral immune tissues, molecules with virus receptor activity may influence whether viruses can access neural, endothelial, epithelial, or immune cells, thereby shaping neuroinflammation, systemic inflammation, blood brain barrier disturbance, and altered neurotransmitter and endocrine regulation. These downstream processes are biologically relevant to depressive illness because depression has repeatedly been associated with inflammatory activation, immune dysregulation, stress system disturbance, and changes in neural plasticity. Therefore, although virus receptor activity is primarily an entry function for pathogens rather than a depression-specific mechanism, it may be viewed as an upstream determinant of infection-related biological events that could contribute indirectly to depression vulnerability or symptom exacerbation.

With this biological context in mind, the currently available evidence should be interpreted cautiously. No relevant publications were provided for direct evaluation, so there is no publication-based evidence in the supplied material that specifically links virus receptor activity to depression. On conceptual biological grounds, however, this functional category may be related to depression indirectly through its role in permitting viral infection, which can trigger peripheral and central immune responses, increase pro-inflammatory cytokine production, alter hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis function, and affect neurotransmitter metabolism and synaptic plasticity, all of which are mechanisms widely implicated in depressive pathophysiology. If a virus gains entry into epithelial, immune, endothelial, or neural cells through host receptors, the resulting infection may promote sickness behavior, persistent inflammation, microglial activation, and disruption of neurovascular integrity, thereby creating conditions that may increase the risk of depressive symptoms or worsen existing depression. In addition, receptor-mediated viral entry in peripheral tissues may contribute to chronic immune activation that communicates with the brain through humoral, neural, and cellular routes, further supporting a plausible but indirect connection between virus receptor activity and depression. Nevertheless, because the present evidence set contains no relevant publications, any asserted relationship remains inferential and should be interpreted cautiously until supported by direct experimental, clinical, or epidemiological studies.

Against this background of indirect biological plausibility, the enrichment results provide a limited but potentially informative point of reference. There were 3 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the function of virus receptor activity. This enrichment count of 3 indicates a small but potentially biologically meaningful host entry module, suggesting that a subset of depression-related proteins may participate in molecular interactions that regulate viral attachment, cellular entry, and the initiation of infection-associated downstream responses. Because virus receptor activity is centered on host factors that determine viral tropism, tissue specificity, and infection efficiency, the identification of 3 proteins in this category supports the interpretation that infection-related host susceptibility mechanisms may intersect with depression biology through inflammatory activation, immune dysregulation, blood brain barrier disruption, cellular stress, and altered neuroendocrine and neurotransmitter regulation. HAVCR1 stands out as the most relevant protein in this list for depression because its annotated functions converge on immune regulation, neuroinflammation, and central nervous system immune cell trafficking, all of which are increasingly implicated in the pathophysiology of depressive disorders. First, HAVCR1 supports regulatory B-cell generation, expansion, and suppressor activity, indicating a role in restraining excessive immune activation (PubMed:21821911, PubMed:25645598, PubMed:32668241). This is potentially important for depression because chronic low-grade inflammation and impaired immunoregulatory tone are frequently observed in subsets of patients with major depressive disorder. Second, HAVCR1 regulates expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines and co-inhibitory ligands, including IL10 (PubMed:25582854, PubMed:25645598). IL10 is of particular interest because reduced anti-inflammatory signaling may contribute to persistent inflammatory states associated with depressive symptoms, sickness behavior, and altered neurotransmission. Third, HAVCR1 acts as a regulator of T-cell proliferation (PubMed:15793576), further supporting a broader role in shaping adaptive immune responses that may influence inflammatory burden. Most notably, HAVCR1 functions as a ligand-related mediator of activated T-cell trafficking during inflammation and controls T-cell accumulation in the inflamed central nervous system as well as induction of autoimmune disease (PubMed:24703780). This central nervous system-directed immune trafficking is especially relevant to depression, as neuroimmune activation, blood-brain barrier-associated immune interactions, and inflammatory effects on neural circuits involved in mood regulation are increasingly recognized as mechanistic contributors to depressive pathology. Although the current evidence does not establish HAVCR1 as a depression gene per se, its combined roles in immune suppression, IL10-associated anti-inflammatory signaling, and central nervous system inflammatory cell recruitment make it a biologically plausible contributor to inflammation-associated depression and a potentially informative marker in disorders where mood symptoms coexist with systemic or neuroinflammatory processes.[PubMed:21821911](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21821911) [PubMed:25645598](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25645598) [PubMed:32668241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668241) [PubMed:24703780](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24703780) [PubMed:25582854](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25582854) [PubMed:15793576](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15793576)

### Splenomegaly (HP:0001744) 

Splenomegaly refers to an abnormal enlargement of the spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ that has central roles in immune surveillance, blood filtration, removal of senescent blood cells, iron recycling, and coordination of innate and adaptive immune responses. Enlargement of the spleen is not a discrete molecular pathway in the strict sense, but rather a clinical and pathological manifestation that commonly reflects systemic immune activation, chronic inflammation, hematologic disturbance, infection, liver disease with portal hypertension, infiltrative disorders, or malignancy. Because the spleen is a major reservoir and regulatory site for monocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes, and cytokine-producing immune cells, splenomegaly often indicates altered peripheral immune homeostasis. In biological terms, this condition can be viewed as a marker of sustained immunologic stress, increased cellular turnover, extramedullary hematopoiesis, or congestion, all of which may influence inflammatory signaling throughout the body. These systemic immune and inflammatory changes are relevant to brain function because peripheral cytokines, immune cell trafficking, neuroendocrine regulation, and communication along humoral and neural routes can affect neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, stress responsivity, and behavior.

In this broader biological context, the potential relevance of splenomegaly to depression is best considered cautiously and through systemic immune mechanisms rather than as a direct disease-specific process. No relevant publications were provided for direct analysis, so there is currently no citation-supported evidence within the supplied material to establish a specific relationship between splenomegaly and depression. Nevertheless, from a biological perspective, splenomegaly may be considered indirectly relevant to depression when it occurs in the setting of chronic systemic inflammation or immune dysregulation, because depression has frequently been associated with altered inflammatory signaling, changes in immune cell activity, and disturbed communication between the peripheral immune system and the central nervous system. In this conceptual framework, an enlarged spleen could reflect persistent activation of immune pathways that may contribute to depressive pathophysiology through increased production of inflammatory mediators, modulation of stress-axis function, and downstream effects on neuronal plasticity and mood regulation. However, splenomegaly itself is a nonspecific clinical finding rather than an established causal mechanism for depression, and without the cited publications there is insufficient basis to determine whether it functions as a comorbid condition, a biomarker of inflammatory burden, or a mechanistic contributor in depressive disease. Therefore, any claimed association should be regarded as hypothetical until supported by direct published evidence.

Against this background, the enrichment results provide a more quantitative basis for considering how this phenotype may intersect with depression-related biology. There were 20 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the function related to splenomegaly, a phenotype that reflects abnormal spleen enlargement and, biologically, points to sustained immune activation, chronic inflammation, altered blood cell turnover, and dysregulated peripheral immune homeostasis. In the context of depression, the enrichment of these 20 proteins supports a quantitatively defined connection between depressive pathology and systemic immune disturbance, particularly because the spleen is a major site for immune cell storage, cytokine production, blood filtration, and coordination of innate and adaptive immune responses. This pattern is biologically relevant because inflammatory signaling arising from splenic and peripheral immune dysregulation can influence brain function through cytokine-mediated communication, immune cell trafficking, and neuroendocrine signaling, thereby affecting stress responsivity, neuroplasticity, neurotransmission, and behavior.

ADA2 is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to depression because adrenergic signaling is centrally involved in stress responsivity, arousal, and mood regulation. By inhibiting adenylate cyclase downstream of catecholamine stimulation, alpha-2 adrenergic receptors reduce intracellular cAMP signaling and modulate presynaptic neurotransmitter release, including norepinephrine. Dysregulation of noradrenergic tone has long been implicated in major depressive disorder, particularly in symptom domains such as impaired motivation, altered attention, psychomotor slowing, sleep disturbance, and exaggerated stress sensitivity. Alpha-2 adrenergic signaling is also relevant to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation and autonomic imbalance, both of which are frequently altered in depression. Therefore, this receptor function stands out as directly connected to canonical neurobiological mechanisms of depressive illness, even though no specific PubMed citation was provided in the input for this entry.

Moving from neurotransmitter regulation to growth and repair signaling, FGFR2 may be relevant because fibroblast growth factor signaling has broad implications for neural development and structural adaptation. FGFR2 is notable because fibroblast growth factor signaling has broad relevance to neurodevelopment, neural plasticity, tissue repair, and cellular resilience, all of which are processes increasingly linked to depression. Although the provided description is general, its roles in cell proliferation and differentiation suggest potential relevance to brain development and the maintenance of neural circuits implicated in affective regulation. Depression has been associated with impaired neuroplasticity and reduced capacity for adaptive remodeling in stress-sensitive brain regions; therefore, proteins involved in growth factor signaling can be mechanistically important. In addition, the mention of wound healing is conceptually relevant because depression is often accompanied by altered inflammatory and reparative responses. FGFR2 thus stands out as a plausible contributor to depression-related biology through effects on developmental programming, structural plasticity, and stress-induced tissue adaptation, although the input does not provide direct citation support for this specific connection.

A related but distinct line of reasoning concerns intracellular metabolism and membrane biology, which brings attention to NPC2. NPC2 is particularly interesting in the context of depression because abnormalities in lipid metabolism, membrane composition, and lysosomal function are increasingly recognized as contributors to psychiatric disease. Cholesterol trafficking is essential for synapse formation, receptor localization, myelination, and membrane microdomain integrity, all of which influence neurotransmission and neuronal signaling. Disruption of intracellular cholesterol handling may therefore affect brain function in ways relevant to mood disorders. Moreover, lysosomal-endosomal dysfunction has emerged as an important theme in neurodegeneration and neuropsychiatric vulnerability, and depression has been linked in some studies to altered cellular metabolism and inflammatory stress that could intersect with sterol trafficking pathways. The secreted role of NPC2 in cholesterol transport also raises the possibility of systemic metabolic contributions, which are relevant because depression commonly co-occurs with metabolic dysregulation. Thus, NPC2 stands out as a mechanistically rich candidate connecting cellular homeostasis, lipid biology, and brain function.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

From cellular metabolism, the discussion naturally extends to barrier integrity, another process that may connect peripheral disturbance with central nervous system effects. OCLN is highly relevant to depression because tight junction biology is fundamental to epithelial and endothelial barrier integrity, including the intestinal barrier and the blood-brain barrier. A growing body of work links depression to barrier dysfunction, increased permeability, peripheral inflammation, and neuroimmune activation. If occludin-mediated tight junction regulation is impaired, this could facilitate the passage of inflammatory mediators or microbial products into the circulation or alter blood-brain barrier homeostasis, thereby contributing to neuroinflammation and altered neuronal function. This is especially important given current models of depression that emphasize gut-brain and immune-brain interactions. Although the input provides only a concise functional annotation and no direct citation, OCLN stands out because barrier disruption is a biologically plausible mechanism linking systemic stress, inflammation, and depressive symptomatology.

In comparison, SCARB2 appears to have a more indirect connection, but it remains of interest when depression is considered within immune and infection-related frameworks. SCARB2 is not a classic depression gene, but it may still be relevant because infection-related and immune-mediated mechanisms can influence depressive phenotypes. The fact that SCARB2 serves as a viral receptor highlights its role at the host-pathogen interface. Infectious exposures can trigger inflammatory cascades, sickness behavior, and in some cases persistent neuroimmune changes that resemble or contribute to depressive symptoms. Beyond the specific annotation provided here, proteins involved in endolysosomal trafficking and pathogen entry are often connected to antigen processing, cellular stress responses, and inflammatory signaling. Therefore, SCARB2 may be of indirect interest in depression research, particularly in frameworks emphasizing infection-triggered immune activation or post-viral neuropsychiatric sequelae. However, compared with ADA2, OCLN, NPC2, and TNFRSF9, the connection is more circumstantial based on the information supplied.

This immune-oriented perspective becomes more direct in the case of TNFRSF9, which may provide a clearer link between inflammatory activation and depression-related mechanisms. TNFRSF9 is one of the strongest depression-relevant proteins in this list because it directly implicates adaptive immune activation, a major contemporary theme in depression pathophysiology. Increasing evidence indicates that at least a subset of patients with depression exhibit chronic low-grade inflammation, altered T-cell phenotypes, and immune-metabolic abnormalities. TNFRSF9 signaling promotes CD8-positive T-cell survival and mitochondrial activity, linking immune effector function with cellular energetics. This is particularly important because mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory activation are both repeatedly implicated in depressive disorders. Enhanced cytotoxic and antiviral immune signaling may be protective in some settings, but persistent or dysregulated activation could contribute to inflammatory states capable of affecting neurotransmitter metabolism, neuroplasticity, and behavior. Accordingly, TNFRSF9 stands out as a biologically meaningful bridge between immune signaling, mitochondrial regulation, and depression-related disease mechanisms, although no specific PubMed citation was provided in the input for this annotation.

Finally, B4GALT1 appears to have a more general and less direct relationship to depression, yet it may still be relevant at the level of post-translational regulation and systemic signaling. B4GALT1 has a less direct connection to depression than several other proteins in this list, but it may still be relevant through its broader role in glycosylation. Glycosylation influences the stability, trafficking, and function of many membrane and secreted proteins, including receptors, adhesion molecules, and immune mediators that can affect brain and systemic physiology. Since altered glycosylation has been implicated in inflammation, cellular communication, and neural signaling, B4GALT1 could theoretically contribute to depression-related biology at the level of post-translational regulation. Nevertheless, based on the provided functional description, its relationship to depression is currently more indirect and speculative than that of proteins involved in neurotransmission, barrier function, cholesterol trafficking, or immune activation.

### cargo receptor activity (GO:0038024) 

Cargo receptor activity is a core membrane trafficking function in which transmembrane proteins selectively recognize luminal or extracellular cargo and couple that cargo to vesicle coat machinery, thereby enabling efficient sorting into newly forming transport vesicles. In secretory and endocytic pathways, cargo receptors operate at membranes such as the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, endosomes, and plasma membrane. Their defining feature is dual recognition: one side of the receptor binds specific cargo molecules, whereas cytoplasmic regions engage coat adaptors and associated trafficking factors, allowing the cargo to be concentrated into vesicles for delivery to the next intracellular compartment. This process is essential for protein quality control, receptor recycling, lysosomal targeting, secretion of signaling molecules, and maintenance of membrane composition. In neural tissue, vesicular sorting is especially important because neurons depend on highly regulated transport of receptors, transporters, neuropeptides, trophic factors, and synaptic membrane components across long cellular distances. Disturbance of cargo receptor mediated trafficking can therefore alter synaptic transmission, cellular stress responses, neurotrophic support, and inflammatory signaling, all of which are biological domains repeatedly implicated in depression. The pathway definition provided here is supported by foundational work on cargo receptor mediated vesicular transport and membrane coat coupling.

Building on this biological framework, the relevance of the pathway to depression should be considered cautiously and in light of the currently available evidence. No pathway specific publications were provided, so there is currently no direct citation based evidence in the supplied literature set linking cargo receptor activity itself to depression. Nonetheless, from a biological standpoint, this pathway is plausibly relevant to depression because mood related brain function depends on accurate intracellular trafficking of membrane proteins and secreted factors. Cargo receptor activity helps determine whether neurotransmitter receptors, transporters, trophic proteins, and stress responsive signaling molecules are properly exported, recycled, degraded, or delivered to synaptic and extrasynaptic membranes. If this sorting function is impaired, neurons and glial cells may show altered synaptic plasticity, defective monoaminergic and glutamatergic signaling, endoplasmic reticulum stress, abnormal neuroimmune communication, and reduced cellular resilience, which are all processes commonly associated with depression pathophysiology. In addition, because cargo receptor systems participate in secretory pathway fidelity and lysosomal delivery, their dysfunction could influence the turnover of proteins that regulate neuronal connectivity and stress adaptation. However, in the absence of depression focused publications in the provided reference list, any disease association should be regarded as mechanistically informed but not directly demonstrated by the supplied evidence. Therefore, the strongest conclusion supported by the current input is that cargo receptor activity represents a biologically credible upstream trafficking pathway that could modulate molecular systems relevant to depression, while direct confirmation requires pathway specific studies in patients with depression or experimental depression models.[PubMed:15239958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15239958) [PubMed:27903609](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27903609) 

With that cautious interpretation in mind, the enrichment result provides a more focused view of how this pathway may intersect with depression associated molecular features. There were 8 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of cargo receptor activity, a membrane trafficking process in which transmembrane receptors selectively bind cargo and couple it to vesicle coat machinery for transport across the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, endosomes, and plasma membrane. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway governs protein quality control, receptor recycling, lysosomal targeting, secretion of signaling molecules, and maintenance of membrane composition, all of which are highly relevant to neural function. In the context of depression, disruption of this trafficking system may influence several quantitatively important disease-related domains, including synaptic transmission, cellular stress responses, neurotrophic support, and inflammatory signaling, since neurons depend on tightly regulated vesicular transport over long cellular distances and across multiple intracellular compartments. The identification of 8 proteins within this pathway therefore supports a focused but potentially meaningful functional module linking membrane sorting biology to depression-associated molecular mechanisms.

To further contextualize these 8 proteins, the interaction network offers a visual summary of their potential functional connectivity. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 8 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

With the network context established, it is useful to examine the individual proteins in greater detail and consider how each may relate, directly or indirectly, to depression relevant biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, FOLR1 stands out as the most directly relevant to depression because folate metabolism is strongly connected to neuropsychiatric function. Folate is essential for one-carbon metabolism, nucleotide synthesis, methylation reactions, and the generation of neurotransmitters, including monoamines that are centrally implicated in depressive disorders. Impaired folate transport or reduced folate availability may contribute to altered methylation capacity, elevated homocysteine, impaired neurodevelopmental and neuroplastic processes, and diminished synthesis of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. These mechanisms are highly plausible in the context of depression, where abnormalities in neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and metabolic support have all been implicated. The described role of FOLR1 in mediating intracellular delivery of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate is therefore particularly important, because this is the biologically active folate form used in central metabolic pathways. Its requirement for normal cell proliferation and embryonic development further supports its broader importance in neural integrity and brain function, while its role in renal folate reabsorption indicates a systemic contribution to maintaining folate homeostasis. Collectively, these features make FOLR1 the most compelling candidate in this list for a meaningful connection to depression, especially in scenarios involving folate deficiency, impaired one-carbon metabolism, or treatment-resistant depressive symptoms associated with metabolic dysregulation.[PubMed:1894617](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1894617) [PubMed:10508523](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10508523) [PubMed:12854656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12854656) [PubMed:15259034](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15259034) [PubMed:17286298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17286298) [PubMed:15703271](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15703271) 

In contrast to FOLR1, which is linked more directly to metabolic and neurotransmitter related mechanisms, COLEC12 appears to be a more indirect but still biologically plausible candidate within the same enriched set. COLEC12 is a plausible, although more indirect, candidate for relevance to depression because its annotated functions converge on innate immunity, vascular biology, oxidative stress, and amyloid-related clearance. Depression is increasingly understood as a disorder in which inflammatory activation, immune dysregulation, and oxidative stress can influence brain function, behavior, and treatment response. In this context, the role of COLEC12 as a scavenger receptor that supports microbial recognition and phagocytosis suggests potential relevance to neuroimmune signaling, particularly given evidence that peripheral immune activation can modulate depressive symptoms. Its ability to mediate endothelial uptake and degradation of oxidized LDL is also noteworthy, because vascular dysfunction and oxidative injury have been linked to depressive phenotypes, especially in late-life and cardiometabolic depression. In addition, the suggestion that COLEC12 may participate in amyloid-beta clearance raises the possibility of relevance to depression associated with neurodegenerative processes, since depressive symptoms frequently accompany prodromal or established neurodegeneration. Although the functional annotation provided does not include direct psychiatric citations, COLEC12 remains biologically interesting because it lies at the intersection of inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and protein clearance pathways that may shape depression risk or symptom burden in specific disease contexts.

### Pleural mesothelioma (WP:WP5087) 

Pleural mesothelioma is a malignant disease arising from the mesothelial lining of the pleura, most commonly linked to prior asbestos exposure. As a disease process, it is characterized by progressive thoracic involvement, respiratory compromise, pain burden, and poor prognosis, and it often requires complex multimodal management such as surgery, systemic treatment, and intensive end-of-life care. The broader pathway context of pleural mesothelioma therefore extends beyond tumor biology alone and includes occupational and environmental causation, compensation and legal issues related to asbestos exposure, substantial financial toxicity, high caregiving demands, and distress surrounding terminal illness. Because pleural mesothelioma is frequently aggressive and socially burdened by preventable exposure history, the disease pathway also encompasses profound psychosocial consequences for both patients and their family members, particularly during bereavement. These features make pleural mesothelioma a clinically important context in which depression may emerge not only from illness severity and caregiving strain, but also from unresolved anger, economic hardship, dissatisfaction with care, and complicated grief after death.  

Against this broader clinical and social background, the available publication suggests that the relationship between pleural mesothelioma and depression is supported primarily through psychosocial and bereavement-related consequences rather than through a direct molecular mechanism. In a survey of bereaved family members of patients who died from malignant pleural mesothelioma in Japan, depression was identified in 19.4 percent of family members, indicating that the pleural mesothelioma care trajectory is associated with a substantial burden of depressive symptoms among survivors of the illness experience. Importantly, depression was more likely among bereaved relatives who were not compensated by the asbestos-related health-damage relief system and among those who experienced financial impacts from the patient’s illness, suggesting that the depression-related effect of pleural mesothelioma may be strongly mediated by socioeconomic stressors embedded within the disease pathway. The same study also showed that dissatisfaction with care during critical illness, lack of compensation, financial burden, and surgical treatment were associated with complicated grief, which is clinically relevant because complicated grief and depression frequently overlap and may reinforce one another in bereavement settings. Taken together, these findings suggest that pleural mesothelioma is related to depression through a multidimensional pathway involving terminal disease burden, caregiving stress, bereavement, financial hardship, and perceived inadequacy of support and care. Thus, in the context of depression, pleural mesothelioma may be understood as a high-risk clinical and social condition that can precipitate depressive outcomes in family members through prolonged emotional strain and structural adversity associated with asbestos-related disease (PubMed:35743451).[PubMed:35743451](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35743451) 

Building on this psychosocial framework, the pathway enrichment results provide an additional molecular layer for interpreting how depression-related biology may intersect with the pleural mesothelioma disease context. There were 18 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing pleural mesothelioma as a malignant pleural disease shaped by asbestos exposure, progressive thoracic deterioration, high symptom burden, poor survival, intensive treatment demands, financial strain, caregiving burden, and bereavement-related psychosocial stress. This enrichment pattern is quantitatively notable because it links depression to a disease context defined not only by severe clinical progression and end-of-life distress, but also by multiple converging nonbiological stressors, including occupational exposure history, compensation-related conflict, economic hardship, dissatisfaction with care, and complicated grief, thereby supporting a multidimensional interpretation of depression risk across patient and family experiences. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 18 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

With this network-level context in place, the function enrichment analysis helps prioritize several proteins whose annotated roles may be relevant to depression. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the proteins listed, MDK stands out as the most directly relevant to depression because it connects several core biological domains implicated in depressive disorders: neuroinflammation, neuroplasticity, neuronal survival, vascular remodeling, and stress-related tissue responses. The protein promotes recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to inflammatory sites and suppresses tolerogenic dendritic-cell development while enhancing T-cell expansion and T helper 1 differentiation, indicating a strong immunomodulatory role. This is notable because major depression is frequently associated with chronic low-grade inflammation, altered innate and adaptive immune signaling, and dysregulated cytokine networks. In parallel, MDK supports neuronal survival, neuronal migration, neurite outgrowth, oligodendroglial precursor elongation, and neural precursor growth through interactions with receptors such as PTPRZ1, SDC3, GPC2, LRP1, integrins, and ALK, and through downstream mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositide 3-kinase signaling. These functions are highly relevant to depression, which has been linked to impaired synaptic plasticity, reduced neurotrophic support, altered connectivity, and abnormalities in glial and white-matter biology. MDK also participates in angiogenesis and endothelial signaling, a potentially important feature given growing evidence that vascular dysfunction and neurovascular unit abnormalities may contribute to depressive symptomatology in some patients. Taken together, MDK is especially compelling because it integrates inflammatory, neurodevelopmental, neurotrophic, and regenerative mechanisms that are central to contemporary models of depression pathophysiology.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

In comparison with MDK, the next group of proteins appears to point more specifically toward structural and signaling mechanisms related to neuronal and vascular plasticity. EFNA1 is noteworthy in the context of depression primarily because of its roles in neuronal structural remodeling and vascular biology. The ability of EFNA1 to evoke embryonic neuronal growth cone collapse and regulate dendritic spine morphogenesis is especially relevant, as depression has repeatedly been associated with altered synaptic architecture, impaired spine dynamics, and maladaptive circuit remodeling in corticolimbic brain regions. Ephrin signaling is a well-established regulator of synapse formation, neuronal connectivity, and activity-dependent plasticity; therefore, EFNA1 may plausibly influence depressive phenotypes through effects on dendritic organization and connectivity. Its role in angiogenesis and endothelial migration is also potentially relevant, since cerebrovascular function and neurovascular coupling are increasingly recognized as contributors to mood disorders. Although the provided annotation emphasizes developmental and cancer-related functions, the neuronal and vascular dimensions of EFNA1 biology make it one of the more plausible proteins on this list to have mechanistic links to depression, particularly through synaptic plasticity and neurovascular regulation.  

Closely related to EFNA1, EPHA2 may be considered within the same signaling axis, but with emphasis on receptor-mediated transduction of these effects. EPHA2 is relevant to depression because Eph receptor signaling has important functions in neuronal connectivity, cytoskeletal regulation, and synaptic remodeling. The annotation indicates that EPHA2 participates in EFNA1-induced RAC1 activation and vascular endothelial cell migration, and that ephrin-Eph signaling can regulate neuronal growth cone collapse and dendritic spine morphogenesis. RAC1-dependent actin remodeling is closely tied to synaptic structure and plasticity, processes that are frequently disrupted in depression. Moreover, Eph receptor pathways can influence how neurons establish and refine contacts, making EPHA2 a plausible mediator of stress-related circuit remodeling. Its vascular functions may add further relevance, as endothelial dysfunction and altered angiogenic signaling have been implicated in subsets of depressive illness. Although the annotation provided for EPHA2 appears to partially duplicate EFNA1-related content, the receptor remains biologically important because it represents the signaling hub through which ephrin-mediated effects on neuronal and vascular plasticity are transduced.  

Shifting from membrane signaling toward transcriptional regulation, YAP1 appears to have a more indirect and lower-confidence connection to depression based on the supplied annotation. YAP1 is potentially relevant despite the limited annotation because its interaction with ERBB4 may connect it to depression-related neurodevelopmental and synaptic mechanisms. ERBB4 is a neurobiologically important receptor in cortical interneuron development and synaptic signaling, and dysregulation of ERBB-family pathways has been implicated in psychiatric disease. Therefore, a protein that activates the ERBB4 C-terminal fragment could influence transcriptional programs, cell survival, or synaptic regulation in neural systems relevant to mood. However, compared with MDK or the ephrin-Eph proteins, the evidence provided here is more limited and indirect. Thus, YAP1 should be viewed as an interesting but lower-confidence candidate whose possible connection to depression would likely depend on broader Hippo-YAP and ERBB4 signaling literature beyond the specific annotation supplied.  

A similarly cautious interpretation applies to MAD1L1, although its potential relevance arises from a different biological domain. MAD1L1 is less directly connected to depression than MDK or the ephrin-Eph signaling proteins, but it remains of interest because disturbances in cell-cycle regulation and genomic stability can influence neurodevelopment and possibly glial biology. The spindle-assembly checkpoint is essential for faithful chromosome segregation, and defects in this pathway can contribute to cellular stress and abnormal tissue development. In depression, especially in developmental or chronic stress contexts, indirect links may arise through altered neurogenesis, gliogenesis, or vulnerability to cellular dysfunction. Nevertheless, based strictly on the supplied functional annotation, MAD1L1 does not map as clearly onto established depression mechanisms as proteins involved in inflammation, neurotrophic support, or synaptic remodeling. It is therefore a secondary candidate rather than a primary mechanistic driver.[PubMed:15024386](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15024386) [PubMed:29162720](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29162720) [PubMed:10700282](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10700282) [PubMed:11804586](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11804586)  

Extending the interpretation beyond neural and developmental biology, FABP4 introduces a possible metabolic and inflammatory dimension to depression-related risk. FABP4 may have a meaningful, albeit indirect, connection to depression through metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Depression is strongly associated with metabolic dysregulation, obesity, altered lipid signaling, and systemic inflammation, and FABP4 is a key mediator of adipocyte lipid handling and retinoid transport. By delivering long-chain fatty acids and retinoic acid to nuclear receptors, FABP4 can influence transcriptional programs related to metabolism and inflammatory state. These processes are relevant because immunometabolic dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a contributor to depressive symptoms in at least a subset of patients. However, the annotation supplied here does not include direct neural or psychiatric functions, so FABP4 should be interpreted as a peripheral systems-level candidate that may shape depression risk through adipose-endocrine and inflammatory mechanisms rather than through direct effects on brain plasticity.  

Finally, EFNA4 returns the discussion to Ephrin-related biology, but with a somewhat more tentative degree of relevance than EFNA1. EFNA4 is of possible interest because it combines developmental Eph-ephrin signaling with a potential immune-cell interaction function. From a depression perspective, the most relevant aspect is likely its participation in neuronal migration, repulsion, and adhesion, since these processes underpin circuit formation and plasticity. Its reported role in activated B-cell and dendritic-cell interactions also raises the possibility of immune relevance, which could be pertinent given the established contribution of immune dysregulation to depression. However, compared with EFNA1, the annotation for EFNA4 provides less explicit evidence for synaptic or neuroplastic functions such as dendritic spine regulation, and therefore its link to depression is more tentative.

### Signaling by Interleukins (REAC:R-HSA-449147) 

Signaling by interleukins is a central component of immune communication that coordinates host defense, tissue repair, hematopoiesis, and the regulation of inflammatory intensity and duration. Interleukins are secreted proteins produced by many cell types, including monocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, adipocytes, and glial cells. After release, they bind to specific cell surface receptors and activate intracellular signaling cascades that alter gene transcription, cellular metabolism, proliferation, differentiation, migration, and survival. Major downstream mechanisms include janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B activation, mitogen activated protein kinase pathways, phosphoinositide three kinase signaling, and inflammasome related processes. Different interleukins exert distinct and sometimes opposing effects. For example, interleukin one, interleukin six, interleukin seventeen, and interleukin eighteen are generally associated with pro inflammatory responses, whereas interleukin four, interleukin ten, and interleukin thirteen contribute to anti inflammatory or inflammation resolving functions depending on cellular context. Because these signals operate in tightly connected networks, signaling by interleukins influences blood brain barrier function, microglial activation, astrocyte responses, neurotransmitter metabolism, neuroendocrine activity, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis. In the nervous system, peripheral and central interleukin signaling can therefore translate immune activation into sustained changes in neural circuits that regulate mood, motivation, cognition, sleep, and stress responsiveness.

Against this biological background, the relevance of this pathway to depression can be considered cautiously on a pathway level, while remaining limited by the absence of publication specific evidence in the provided materials. No relevant publications were provided in the input list, so a publication specific analysis cannot be performed and no citation supported causal interpretation should be claimed from the supplied evidence. Nevertheless, based on the established biological role of signaling by interleukins, this pathway appears highly plausible in depression because depression is frequently accompanied by a state of low grade systemic and central inflammation characterized by altered concentrations of several interleukins. Increased signaling by pro inflammatory interleukins can affect the brain through multiple converging mechanisms, including promotion of microglial activation, impairment of blood brain barrier integrity, stimulation of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal stress system, alteration of monoamine synthesis and turnover through inflammation linked metabolic pathways, reduction of neurotrophic support, and disruption of synaptic plasticity and hippocampal neurogenesis. At the same time, insufficient anti inflammatory interleukin activity may weaken compensatory mechanisms that normally restrain inflammatory damage and restore homeostasis. Through these processes, interleukin signaling may contribute to anhedonia, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbance, and stress sensitivity, all of which are prominent features of depression. However, because no relevant publications were supplied, the present conclusion should be regarded as a biologically informed pathway level interpretation rather than a literature grounded synthesis tied to the provided references.

Building on this general biological rationale, the enrichment results provide a quantitative context for why this pathway may warrant attention in depression related analyses. There were 20 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of signaling by interleukins. This enrichment is biologically notable because interleukin signaling integrates multiple immune regulatory layers, including host defense, tissue repair, hematopoiesis, and the control of inflammatory intensity and duration, while also influencing central nervous system processes that are highly relevant to depression, such as blood brain barrier regulation, microglial activation, astrocyte reactivity, neurotransmitter metabolism, neuroendocrine signaling, synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and stress responsiveness. Across these 20 proteins, the pathway context supports a quantitatively meaningful immune centered interpretation of depression biology, since signaling by interleukins includes both pro inflammatory mediators, such as interleukin one, interleukin six, interleukin seventeen, and interleukin eighteen, and anti inflammatory or inflammation resolving mediators, such as interleukin four, interleukin ten, and interleukin thirteen, indicating that at least 7 major interleukin classes with partly opposing effects can converge on shared downstream signaling routes, including janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B activation, mitogen activated protein kinase signaling, phosphoinositide three kinase signaling, and inflammasome related processes. This functional profile is consistent with the view that depression is associated not only with altered inflammatory magnitude, but also with dysregulation in the balance, duration, and cellular context of immune signaling, which can translate peripheral immune activation into persistent changes in neural circuits governing mood, motivation, cognition, and sleep.

With this network level view in place, it is helpful to turn to individual proteins that may contribute to the biological interpretation of the enrichment results. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following. SOD2 is a mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme that catalyzes the detoxification of superoxide radicals, thereby limiting oxidative stress and protecting cellular macromolecules from damage. This function is highly relevant to depression because convergent evidence implicates oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation in the pathophysiology of depressive disorders. Neurons are especially vulnerable to reactive oxygen species due to their high metabolic demand, and impaired antioxidant defense can contribute to synaptic dysfunction, altered neuroplasticity, and reduced cellular resilience in brain regions implicated in mood regulation, such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. As the principal mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, SOD2 stands out as a biologically meaningful protein because it directly links mitochondrial redox homeostasis to mechanisms frequently observed in depression, including inflammatory activation and stress-related cellular injury. Thus, altered SOD2 activity or expression could plausibly influence depression risk, severity, or treatment response through its effects on oxidative balance and neuronal integrity.
